title: Santorini
description: A volcanic island in the Aegean where vines grow in baskets and Assyrtiko keeps its acidity in fierce sun.
L: Santorini is a Greek island in the southern Aegean, in the Cyclades. Around 1600 BC, one of the largest volcanic eruptions in human history blew out its centre, leaving a crescent-shaped island around a flooded caldera. Vineyards cover about 1,100 hectares, on the gentle outer slopes.

Santorini's soil, called aspa, is volcanic ash, pumice, lava and pieces of rock, with almost no clay or organic matter. It's very poor and drains instantly. Phylloxera can't survive in it, so vines are ungrafted and roots can be centuries old. The pumice holds a little moisture, helping roots through summer.
Phylloxera can't survive in volcanic aspa
The volcanic soil keeps phylloxera out.

Santorini is hot and very dry, with about 300 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Strong winds, including the meltemi in summer, blow constantly. Vines rely on night-time sea mist and dew for moisture. Yields are tiny, often 10 to 20 hl/ha, among the lowest in Europe.
Not true. It's very dry; vines rely on sea mist and dew.
Santorini is a crescent around a volcanic caldera

Assyrtiko covers about 80% of Santorini's vineyards. It keeps very high acidity even when fully ripe in strong sun, a rare trait. It gives bone-dry whites with lemon, lime, flint, smoke and a saline edge, with high alcohol. Santorini PDO white must be at least 75% Assyrtiko.

Athiri adds citrus and floral softness; Aidani adds floral, honeyed aromas. Both are blended with Assyrtiko and used in Vinsanto. Red grapes, like Mandilaria and Mavrotragano, a rare local grape, are also grown, mainly for reds and some Vinsanto.
Match each grape to its role.
Nykteri, from the Greek for night, was traditionally made from grapes picked at night and oak-aged. It's a richer style of Santorini Assyrtiko.
It keeps high acidity in hot sun

Explain the threat to Santorini's vineyards

Santorini's vines are trained into kouloura, low baskets woven from the vine's own canes, lying on the ground. The grapes grow inside the basket. Each year, new canes are woven in, so the basket grows. After 50 to 80 years, the basket is cut off, and a new one grows from the same old roots.

The kouloura protects grapes from strong winds, which can strip leaves and fruit, from fierce sun and from blowing volcanic sand. Inside, the grapes catch moisture from night sea mist and dew, the vines' main water source. The low shape keeps the vines close to the cooler, more humid ground.
Shelter from wind, sun and sand
What does the kouloura protect against?
Santorini has mild winters; frost isn't the main concern.

Santorini's vineyards are shrinking. Tourism has made land extremely valuable, and many vineyards have been built on. Low yields, drought and climate change add pressure. Producers like Hatzidakis, Gaia, Sigalas and Santo Wines work to protect the vines and their heritage.

Reading Santorini and eating with it

Labels show Santorini PDO, the producer and sometimes Nykteri or a single vineyard. Vinsanto, Santorini's sweet wine, is made from at least 51% Assyrtiko with Aidani, from grapes sun-dried for about 12 to 14 days, then fermented and aged at least two years in oak, often much longer. It's amber, with raisin, apricot, coffee and spice, balanced by acidity.

Dry Assyrtiko suits Greek seafood: grilled octopus, sea bass, squid, shellfish, and local dishes like fava, a yellow split pea purée, tomatokeftedes, tomato fritters, and feta. Its acidity cuts through olive oil. Vinsanto suits dried fruit, nuts, blue cheese and chocolate. Serve Assyrtiko at 8 to 11 degrees.
From sun-dried grapes, aged in oak
Top Santorini Assyrtiko ages well for 10 to 15 years, gaining smoky, honeyed notes while keeping its acidity.
Dry Assyrtiko is a good match for grilled octopus.
Yes. Its acidity and saltiness suit grilled seafood.
